title: Register: degrees of formality
subtitle: spectacles / glasses / specs
summary: Match your words to the situation: neutral, formal and informal sets such as spectacles-glasses-specs, words tied to speech or writing, and words that now sound archaic.

lesson.heading: What register means
lesson.text: **Register** is the overall tone of a text or conversation and the relationship it builds between speaker and listener, or writer and reader. Some words are formal, some informal, and many are quite neutral. It is important to speak and write in the register the situation calls for.

examples.text: Is your **partner** not with you today?
examples.note: partner is neutral; other half is informal
bloke and guy are informal words for man

examples.text: She is able to **converse** with everyone, which is a great gift.
examples.note: converse is the formal word for have a conversation

lesson.heading: Neutral, formal and informal sets
rows: have a go / stab / bash / crack / shot at

lesson.heading: The same sentence in two registers

left.label: More formal
examples: She works in a shop that sells women's **clothing**.
I spent the morning **conversing** with the Director.
The company will **endeavour** to **ensure** that all data is protected.

right.label: More informal
examples: I've got some new **specs**. Do you like them?
Did you see that documentary about Wales on the **telly** last night?
Gerry's a decent **bloke**. I wouldn't want to upset him.

lesson.note: Between them sits the neutral version: Molly was there with her husband. He's a nice man.

lesson.heading: Words that belong to writing (W) or speech (S)
columns: What it does and an example
rows: linking adverb; in speech we would say later or afterwards: The police found some important clues. **Subsequently**, three people were arrested.
linking expression meaning to sum up: **In sum**, we may say that most, but not all, English adverbs end in -ly.
vague word used when you cannot remember a person's name: I met **whatsername** at the party, the woman who works at the university.
vague noun for people and things whose name you cannot remember: Give me that **thingy** there, yes, that bottle opener.
discourse marker bringing attention to an important point: He's a good actor. **Mind you**, he should be - he went to the best drama college.
discourse marker used to get people's attention: **Now then**, is everybody's luggage here?
lesson.note: Frequently, begin and moreover are far commoner in writing; start and maybe are far commoner in speech.

lesson.heading: Outdated words
lesson.text: Some words and expressions are correct but sound **archaic** - outdated or old-fashioned. Using them today would strike your listener as odd, or deliberately literary.

examples.text: **asylum** - the old word for a hospital for the mentally ill
**frock** for dress, **wireless** for radio, **eyeglasses** for glasses
**consumption** - the old word for tuberculosis or TB
**apothecary** for pharmacist, **damsel** for girl, **poesy** for poetry, **whither** for where to

lesson.heading: Recognising register in a text
rows: When you have created a file that is to be stored in a shared folder, or one that is located on a server, you can use the tools in the client software to restrict access to the file.
shared folder, server, located, and the passive voice
Views are certainly divided on the answers to the questions listed above; even whether it matters that pluralism and different paradigms reign in SLA is a matter of heated debate.
listed above, paradigms, the initials SLA
Sweetest love, I do not go, For weariness of thee, Nor in hope the world can show A fitter love for me.
thee for you, weariness, and elsewhere 'tis and feigned
And so, my fellow Americans: ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.
ask not instead of don't ask, my fellow, the freedom of man
Mind you there was a lot of rain in Germany over Christmas wasn't there, cos I saw the river in Bonn on the news on telly, the Rhine.
mind you, cos, telly, and the fragmented, unjoined sentences

lesson.text: When you learn a new word, note whether it is neutral - neutral words are safe everywhere, while formal and informal ones are only right in the right situation.

exercises.prompt: Make this more formal: She works in a shop that sells women's ___.
exercises.explanation: Clothing and garments are the formal equivalents of clothes.

exercises.prompt: Make this informal: I've got some new ___. Do you like them?
exercises.explanation: Spectacles is formal, glasses neutral and specs informal.

exercises.prompt: Make this informal: Did you see that documentary about Wales on the ___ last night?
exercises.explanation: The telly and the box are both informal words for television.

exercises.prompt: Make this informal: Gerry's a decent ___. I wouldn't want to upset him.
exercises.explanation: Bloke and guy are informal words for man.

exercises.prompt: Make this formal: I spent the morning ___ with the Director.
exercises.explanation: Converse is the formal verb for have a conversation.

exercises.prompt: Make this neutral: Molly was there with her ___. He's a nice man.
exercises.explanation: Other half is informal; husband and partner are neutral.

exercises.prompt: Is each word formal or informal?
Match each neutral word with its formal equivalent.
Is each word much more common in everyday speech or in everyday writing?
Which linking word would you expect in a written report rather than in conversation?
exercises.explanation: Subsequently is a written linking adverb; in speech we say later or afterwards.

exercises.prompt: He's a good actor. ___, he should be - he went to the best drama college.
exercises.explanation: Mind you is a spoken discourse marker that brings attention to an important point.

exercises.prompt: ___, we may say that most, but not all, English adverbs end in -ly.
exercises.explanation: In sum is a written linking expression meaning to sum up.

exercises.prompt: Match each outdated word with its present-day equivalent.

exercises.statement: Consumption was once the everyday word for tuberculosis.
exercises.explanation: Correct - consumption is now archaic; we say tuberculosis or TB.

exercises.statement: The words cos, telly and yeah suggest a formal written text.
exercises.explanation: They mark informal modern conversation; a written text would have because, television and yes.
